design: Written for the open pack from real geography; nothing comes from the original game. How the engine uses them (src/sim/treasure.c, src/ui/screens.c): a new map takes a random spot whose nearest town (by the era's arrival cells) is neither the player's town nor another map's, and names that town ("Somewhere near ..."). The map shows the 40 x 30 cells around the spot. A party ashore digs it up when it stands within one cell of it, both ways (|dx| < 2 and |dy| < 2 cells); the party walks on land pixels only, from where its ship touched the shore. One table serves every era. Where. The places the rovers of 1560-1680 and their legends used: small cays and islands, headlands, river mouths and lagoon shores away from the settled ports. ANCHORS below names each one with real coordinates (degrees, modern) and how many spots it gets: the Florida Keys and capes, the Gulf coast (Barataria, Sabine Pass, the Tamaulipas and Veracruz lagoons, Laguna de Terminos), Yucatan's capes and Cozumel, the Belize cays and the Bay Islands (Roatan, Utila, Guanaja), the Mosquito coast (Cabo Gracias a Dios, the Pearl Cays, Bluefields' lagoons, Bocas del Toro), the San Blas islands and the Darien, the Main's capes, the Dutch islands, the Venezuelan islands and the Paria coast, Trinidad, the Grenadines and the Windwards, Barbuda, Anegada and St Croix, Puerto Rico's islets (Mona, Desecheo, Vieques, Caja de Muertos), around Hispaniola (Saona, Samana, La Isabela, Tortuga's west end, Gonave, Ile-a-Vache, the Tiburon peninsula), Cuba's cays and bays (Isla de Pinos, Jardines de la Reina, Cayo Romano, the Colorados), Jamaica's capes and bays (Negril, Morant Point), the Caymans, the Bahamas and the Caicos, and the Atlantic shore from Biscayne Bay to Cape Fear. Bigger or more storied haunts get more spots (Isla de Pinos 5, Andros 4). The tiniest islets (the Virgin islands but Anegada and St Croix, Saba, Navassa, the lower Keys and the Dry Tortugas, Turneffe, Cayo Largo, Los Testigos, San Andres, the Swan islands) are left out: the open map's 16-pixel cells, about 7 km, draw them as a few pixels of land that no cell can hold as a dig site, and their spots went to the larger islands' shores. Snapping. Each anchor goes through _geo.lonlat_to_world() and takes the fitting cells of the map nearest to it, up to 7 cells (50 km) away, as many as its count; the anchors with the fewest fitting cells per spot choose first, so a lone cay keeps its cell before a neighbour's coast spreads over it. A cell fits when, in every era's map (the bare map, world_map.base_grid(), with that era's town houses drawn on it, tables/towns.py): an eighth of its pixels or more are land a landing party can stand on (land 4-connected to sea that is itself joined to the open sea without crossing shallows, so any ship reaches the shore without passing a reef), as the towns' coastal cells (the map's tiles draw a small cay as a corner of land, never a whole cell), a cell less than half land counting one cell farther, so a bigger island's solid ground wins over its fringe; a cell with open sea of the main water (64 pixels or more, as the towns' reach) lies within 3 cells, so the spot is a short walk from where a ship can come in and the map's 40 x 30 cells always show a shoreline; it is 2 cells or more (Chebyshev) from every arrival cell of every era's towns, so the spot is near a named town but never in it and a party digging there never walks into a town; it is 3 cells or more from every other spot, so no two dig areas (the 3 x 3 cells around a spot) overlap; and it keeps 6 cells from the map's edge. 217 anchors; snapped 1.6 cells from their anchors on average, 6.4 at most; the named town's arrival cells 2 to 199 cells away (|dx| + |dy|, over the eras), median 23.
